title: Kaplan's God
hookLine: Kaplan pictured God as the power in the world that makes for goodness and fulfillment

lines: A CRAYON GOD ON THE FRIDGE.
cards: On a refrigerator door, a child's crayon drawing: a giant in the clouds with a long white beard, over a small house with a crooked chimney. Ask the artist who that is, and the answer comes fast. God.
Some grown-ups still carry that drawing inside them, never revised.

Mordecai Kaplan, the thinker behind the Reconstructionist movement, asked a different question: not where God lives, or what God looks like, but what God does in a human life. His answer is today's word.

teach.h: NO CARVED IMAGE. I AM THAT I AM.
teach.b: Kaplan's God. The Torah forbids carving an image of God. You met the name from the burning bush on day eighty-two.
In the King James words it is "I AM THAT I AM," and some readers hear the Hebrew as I will be what I will be, a name that won't sit still for a portrait.

Maimonides taught that one can say only what God is not, because every positive description falls short. Kabbalists spoke of Ein Sof, the without-end. So Kaplan stepped into an old conversation; he did not start it.
He set aside the idea of a God who reaches in from outside nature to work miracles.

teach.h: THE POWER THAT MAKES FOR GOODNESS.
teach.b: He described God as the power in the world that makes for salvation, and by salvation he meant goodness and fulfillment in this life: the pull toward honesty, the force that lets a wounded thing heal, the energy that moves people to build fairer lives together.
On this view you meet God less as a voice from the sky and more when people take up Micah's charge "to do justly, and to love mercy."
Believing in God, for Kaplan, meant trusting that the world holds that power, and joining it.

teach.h: FREEING TO SOME, TOO THIN TO OTHERS.
teach.b: Some readers found his picture freeing, a way to keep praying with honest words. Others, in several movements, replied that a power is not someone who hears, and a prayer needs a listener.
Reconstructionist Jews today hold a range of views, and not all follow Kaplan here.
His idea leaves a question, not a verdict: what does a picture of God do in the life of the one who holds it?

how: Reconstructionist prayer books and teachers often invite worshippers to bring their own understanding of God to prayer, and Kaplan's idea of God as the power that makes for goodness is one of the views discussed in the movement.

games.q: you're Mordecai Kaplan. people tell you they can no longer pray to a giant in the clouds. what do you offer them?
o: a picture of God as the power in the world that makes for goodness.
tell them to keep the old picture and stop asking.
games.why: Kaplan described God as the power that makes for salvation, meaning goodness and fulfillment in this life. some found it freeing; others said a power cannot hear a prayer.

practice: Let the word God come to mind, and see what arrives with it: a face, a light, an empty space, a warmth, a doubt, or nothing at all. Just notice it, and ask where that picture came from.
If you pray, you can pray in silence to God as you understand God; if you don't, let the picture be there for a while, then let it go.

wordCard.voice: Kaplan's God. The power in the world that makes for goodness and fulfillment: one picture of God among several in Jewish thought. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: many ways to picture God. Kaplan's is one, in a very old conversation. Another week, complete.
